summary: This instructional talk treats Photoshop and post-processing as a creative tool to expand options for landscape imagery while emphasizing ethical boundaries. The presenter contrasts the eye’s perception with a camera’s limitations in dynamic range and motion, arguing that successful post-processing should simplify complex scenes, create visual flow from near to far, and guide the viewer toward the image’s light source. Core concepts include structuring images with framing, leading lines, and layers; building transitions that push the eye toward highlights; and using atmospheric diffusion, edge control, and tonal separation (levels of blacks) to convey depth. The speaker demonstrates practical techniques for achieving three-dimensionality with long and short lenses, including strategically placing light, dodge-and-burn edits, and pre-dawn lighting strategies, and repeatedly emphasizes deliberate cropping and spacing (the “rule of six”) to avoid distracting empty space. Real-world location examples (Death Valley, Pakistan, Rainbow Mountain in Peru, Santa Barbara, Bishop, Olympic National Park, Canadian Rockies) anchor the discussion in practice while illustrating how to apply these principles across diverse landscapes.

sections.title: Philosophy and boundaries of Photoshop
concepts: Photoshop as a tool to increase options
Not all shots need post-processing (highly successful as-is)
Only certain shots benefit from editing (two-to-nine conversions)
sections.description: The speaker frames Photoshop as expanding creative options, while defining boundaries: avoid altering permanently recognizable scene elements and acknowledge that some images should not be edited.

sections.title: Eye vs. camera: dynamic range and motion
concepts: Eye perceives dynamic range differently from cameras
Motion and movement affect perceived depth
Strategic editing to compensate for camera limitations
sections.description: Two ways the eye sees differently than the camera—dynamic range and motion—are introduced as the basis for post-processing decisions to regain sense of depth and realism.

sections.title: Visual flow and depth creation
concepts: Creating a three-dimensional feel
Directing viewer from near to far
Simplifying complex landscapes through motion cues
sections.description: The presenter explains why visual flow and motion cues matter, describing how research into near-to-far relationships guides composition and viewer immersion.

sections.title: Foundational composition structures
concepts: Framing, leading lines, and layers
Layered compositions as a recurring theme on this trip
Transitions that guide light toward focal points
sections.description: Overview of framing, leading lines, and layers as the basic structures from which transitions and depth are built.

sections.title: Transitions and light-focused composition
concepts: Light as the focal guide
Level of blacks transitions to create depth
Big-to-small transitions and foreground-to-background depth
sections.description: Emphasizes how transitions direct attention toward the light source and how tonal transitions shape perceived depth, with repeated emphasis on big-to-small relationships.

sections.title: Practical examples and applications
concepts: Case studies across locations (Pakistan, Peru, Santa Barbara, etc.)
45-degree angle for foreground-to-background depth
Atmosphere and diffusion to separate foreground and background
sections.description: Shows multiple illustrative edits across locations, underscoring the 45-degree foreground-to-background technique and the use of atmosphere to enhance depth.

sections.title: Long-lens depth and lighting tactics
concepts: Long-lens tricks to emulate wide-angle depth
Adding left-side light and shading toward it
Dodge-and-burn to reveal three-dimensional form
sections.description: Explains how long-lens shots can achieve the dramatic depth and light dynamics typically associated with wide-angle images, plus brief post-processing moves to enhance depth.

sections.title: Backlight and sun-forward forest strategy
concepts: Backlighting reduces distracting shadows
Shooting into the sun to simplify the scene
Using sun-star and edge hints to guide the eye
sections.description: Discusses backlighting in forest scenes, strategies for minimizing distractions, and how light direction shapes composition.

sections.title: Rule of odds, edge control, and closing tips
concepts: Rule of odds and focal-point tension
Space usage and cropping (the 'rule of six')
Edge control and cropping out distractions
sections.description: Wraps with composition diagnostics, crop decisions, and edge considerations, plus a final note on keeping the subject’s focal point intact.
